title: Law
tagline: The meaning of law, its sources from custom to legislation, and its kinds from municipal to international law.

overview.intro: Law is the instrument through which a political order states what it permits, forbids and requires, and through which disputes are settled without force. This unit examines what law is, the sources from which it draws its authority — custom, usage, religion, judicial decisions, scientific commentaries, equity and legislation — and the kinds of law that apply from the municipal level to relations between states.

facts.label: Meaning
facts.value: A rule of conduct prescribed by the sovereign and enforced by the state, or more broadly any rule that a legal system recognises as binding.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Custom and usage, religion, judicial decisions, scientific commentaries, equity, and legislation.

facts.label: Kinds
facts.value: Municipal (constitutional, criminal, civil, administrative) and international law.

facts.label: Central problem
facts.value: Whether law derives its authority from the sovereign alone or also from morality and custom.

learningOutcomes: Define law and explain its purpose in a political community.
Describe the sources of law and their relative weight.
Distinguish the kinds of municipal law.
Explain the relationship between municipal and international law.
Assess whether law without moral content can still be called law.

blocks.text: Law may be defined as a rule of conduct laid down and enforced by the recognised authority of a political community, so that human relations within it are ordered rather than settled by force. In the analytical tradition associated with Austin, law is the command of the sovereign enforced by a sanction; in the historical tradition it is the custom of the community crystallised by the courts; and in the sociological view it is any rule that a court would apply. The common element across the definitions is enforceability through recognised procedure, which separates a legal obligation from a moral or conventional one.

The purposes of law follow from that. It settles disputes through stated procedure instead of self-help; it protects persons, property and expectations so that long-term planning is possible; it enables collective action by authorising the state to tax, regulate and compel; and it restrains power itself, since a government that must act through published rules is easier to hold to account than one that acts by discretion. Law is therefore both the instrument of authority and its limit, which is why the same body of rules can serve opposite political purposes depending on how they are written and who administers them.

blocks.text: Custom is the oldest source: a practice observed over time acquires the force of law when it is certain, reasonable, continuous and not opposed to statute. Usage differs from custom in being the settled practice of a particular trade or locality, which merchants’ law absorbed long before legislation regulated commerce. Religion supplied sacred law in many systems, governing marriage, inheritance and personal status, and in some polities religious rules remain directly binding in those fields.

Judicial decisions supply law through precedent: the doctrine of stare decisis holds that a court is bound by the reasoning of an earlier court on a similar material fact, which gives the law certainty at the cost of some rigidity. Scientific commentaries — the writings of recognised jurists — do not bind, but courts cite them as persuasive authority, particularly where statute is silent. Equity arose to soften the harshness of common law, developing doctrines such as specific performance and trust, and in most modern systems it has been fused with the ordinary courts while retaining its distinct principles. Legislation is the dominant modern source: a rule enacted by the competent law-making body, which can create, alter or repeal any rule beneath it and is the only source that can override the others.

learn.title: Kinds of law: municipal and international

blocks.text: Municipal law is the law of a single state and its several branches. Constitutional law defines the institutions of the state, distributes powers among them and states the rights of citizens against authority. Criminal law defines offences and prescribes punishment, and rests on the principle that there can be no crime and no punishment without a pre-existing law. Civil law governs relations between persons — contract, property, family and tort — and provides remedies rather than punishment. Administrative law controls the exercise of executive power through procedure, reasons and review, which is the branch that most directly limits government in daily practice.

International law governs relations between states and, in modern usage, certain international organisations and individuals. It arises from treaty, custom and general principles, and its subjects are primarily states rather than persons. The classic distinction is that municipal law is enforced by the physical power of the state while international enforcement depends largely on reciprocity, institutions and, in the last resort, collective measures — which is why earlier writers denied it the name of law altogether. The modern view is that enforcement is a matter of degree: a rule that states treat as binding, that their courts apply and that institutions adjudicate is law in the relevant sense, even though it lacks a world sovereign to command it.

blocks.caption: Municipal against international law
rows: Persons and bodies within the state
Courts backed by the physical power of the state
Binding principally through consent of states

blocks.text: The relation between law and freedom is not simply opposition. A law that forbids theft restricts one person’s liberty in order to secure everyone’s, and the liberal answer, drawn from Kant and Green, is that law is not the opposite of freedom but its condition, since rules which apply to all equally create the space in which each may act. Rousseau’s formula points the same way: obedience to a law prescribed to oneself as a member of the sovereign is self-rule. The genuine danger lies not in law as such but in law that is secret, retrospective or arbitrary — which is why legality demands that rules be published, prospective, general and applied by an independent court.

The principal criticism of the analytical position is that an immoral law may still satisfy Austin’s definition, since apartheid legislation and retrospective statutes were commands of a sovereign and were enforced. The natural-law reply is that such enactments are badly law or not law at all, and the legal-positivist reply, defended by Hart, is that law and morality must be separated in order to criticise law honestly: we can say a rule is legally valid and morally intolerable, and the two questions should not be blurred. The debate matters politically because it decides whether officials may refuse to apply a rule on the ground that it is unjust, and most constitutional systems have answered by giving courts the power of review while insisting that ordinary officials obey.

items: Law restrains power as well as commanding obedience.
Custom and usage operate as sources wherever statute is silent.
Precedent gives certainty; legislation gives change.
International law is law with weaker enforcement, not law without enforcement.
Legality requires rules to be published, prospective, general and impartially applied.

keyPoints: Law is a rule of conduct enforced by the recognised authority of a political community.
It settles disputes, protects persons and property, enables collective action and restrains power.
Custom requires certainty, reasonableness, continuity and no conflict with statute.
Precedent binds through stare decisis while commentary is only persuasive.
Equity developed to correct the harshness of common law and has been fused with it.
Legislation is the supreme source and can create, alter or repeal any rule beneath it.
Municipal law divides into constitutional, criminal, civil and administrative branches.
International law derives from treaty, custom and general principles and binds states principally by consent.
International enforcement rests on reciprocity and institutions rather than a world sovereign.
The central dispute is whether law and morality must be separated for either to be judged honestly.
examFocus: Sources questions need each source with its character and weight, not a bare list.
Municipal/international comparison is best given as a table on four bases.
The law-and-freedom answer should distinguish legality from the content of particular laws.

Doctrine that courts are bound by the reasoning of earlier decisions.
Principles developed to correct the harshness of strict legal rules.

questions.prompt: The source of law that can create, alter or repeal any other source is:
questions.explanation: Legislation is the supreme source because it is enacted by the competent law-making body and overrides the others.

questions.prompt: The doctrine that a court is bound by the reasoning of an earlier court on similar material facts is:
questions.explanation: Precedent gives the law certainty, though courts may depart from it with justification.

questions.prompt: Which branch of municipal law directly controls the exercise of executive power?
questions.explanation: Administrative law subjects official action to procedure, reasons and judicial review.

questions.prompt: The principal difference between municipal and international law lies in:
options: Enforcement: municipal law is backed by the physical power of the state, international law by reciprocity and institutions
questions.answer: Enforcement: municipal law is backed by the physical power of the state, international law by reciprocity and institutions
questions.explanation: Both are rules recognised as binding, but enforcement mechanisms differ fundamentally, which is what earlier critics seized on.

questions.prompt: A practice observed over time that is certain, reasonable and continuous acquires the force of __________ .
questions.explanation: Custom operates as a source of law wherever legislation is silent.

questions.prompt: The branch of municipal law that defines offences and prescribes punishment is __________ law.
questions.explanation: Criminal law rests on the principle that there can be no crime and no punishment without a law that made it an offence in advance.

questions.prompt: State four purposes of law in a political community.
questions.answer: Four purposes are: to settle disputes through stated procedure instead of self-help; to protect persons, property and expectations so that people can plan; to enable collective action by authorising the state to tax, regulate and compel; and to restrain power itself, since authority exercised through published rules can be accounted for. Predictability of consequences is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each purpose must be explained by the mechanism through which law achieves it.

questions.prompt: Describe four sources of law and state the weight each carries.
questions.answer: Custom is a practice observed over time that is certain, reasonable and continuous; it binds wherever statute is silent. Judicial decisions operate through precedent, under which lower courts are bound by the reasoning of higher courts on similar material facts, giving certainty. Scientific commentaries by recognised jurists do not bind but are cited as persuasive authority, particularly where statute is silent. Legislation is an enactment by the competent law-making body and is supreme: it can create, alter or repeal any rule beneath it and overrides all other sources. Equity, developed to correct the harshness of common law, is applied alongside it and is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Four sources must each be described with the weight they carry relative to legislation.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between law and freedom, and assess whether law necessarily limits liberty.
questions.answer: The naive view holds that law and freedom stand opposed, since every rule forbids something and therefore narrows the range of action. The classical political answer is more subtle and takes two forms. The liberal form, associated with Kant and Green, argues that law is the condition rather than the enemy of freedom: a rule that binds everyone equally, including the powerful, removes the arbitrary interference that actually prevents people from acting, so the person protected from another’s caprice is freer than the person in a condition where force decides. Rousseau’s formula points the same way from a different direction, holding that obedience to a law the citizen prescribes to himself as a member of the sovereign is self-rule rather than subjection. On this account it is not law that limits liberty but lawlessness, since in the absence of rules the stronger impose their will without restraint. The qualification is that this holds only of law that meets the standards of legality — published, prospective, general and applied by an independent court. Retrospective statutes, secret rules and laws aimed at named persons restrict liberty without creating the mutual security that justifies restriction, and the twentieth century supplied abundant examples. The assessment therefore has to separate law in general from bad law: law necessarily limits particular actions, and where it does so to secure the conditions of action for all it enlarges freedom overall, but where it departs from generality and publicity it becomes merely organised power. A strong answer states the principle, applies the test of legality, and judges particular laws by whether they create mutual security or special disability.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the two forms of the positive answer, the test of legality, and a judgement distinguishing general law from arbitrary enactment.

questions.prompt: “An unjust law is not a law at all.” Discuss with reference to the natural law and legal positivist positions.
questions.answer: The statement is the classic natural-law claim, and its force is that it refuses to let legality settle moral questions. Natural lawyers argue that law draws its authority from its conformity with a higher standard — reason, natural rights or justice — so a rule that commands atrocity, or that is retrospective and aimed at named persons, fails in what makes a rule law and may properly be disobeyed. The evidence for the position includes the conduct of officials who refused to apply racial statutes and the intuition that the Nuremberg prosecutions required some standard above the enacted law of the regime. Legal positivism answers that the two questions must be kept apart. Austin and especially Hart argue that validity depends on the rule’s pedigree — enacted by the competent authority and recognised within the system — not on its merits, and that mixing the questions makes honest criticism impossible: one can say precisely that a rule is legally valid and morally abominable, which is a stronger indictment than saying it was never law. The positivist also points to the practical difficulty: if each official may decline a rule they consider unjust, legal certainty collapses and the office becomes a licence. The natural lawyer replies that a system of exactly ordered commands issuing from a tyranny shows that procedural validity cannot be the whole of law, and that the positivist’s own distinction between primary and secondary rules smuggles in standards the system must meet. The most defensible conclusion is that the dispute turns on what the word law is being asked to do: as a description of validity in a functioning legal system the positivist is right that morality is not a criterion of validity; as a claim about authority and obligation the natural lawyer is right that a command which flouts the most basic standards forfeits the duty to obey. Recognising that the two answers address different questions resolves most of the argument, while leaving genuinely hard cases where officials must decide whether to act on their judgement.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both positions stated in their strongest form, evidence from a concrete case, and a conclusion that shows the question has two dimensions.
